newsitem.title: CHINA: Price, not drought, affects China's cotton market.
newsitem.headline: Price, not drought, affects China's cotton market.

text.p: The cotton crop in China's Shandong province is unlikely to be hit by the drought sweeping the country's north, particularly as rains have helped ease the pressure, trade sources said on Thursday.
"The weather is not an issue, as a matter of fact, the recent rains that have fallen ... are beneficial to the cotton crop," said one cotton source.
Instead, China's cotton industry pricing structure was a far more important issue for the market, traders said.
Analysts have said that pest attacks, pollution and bad weather have contributed to projections of a lower cotton crop.
But main problem remained China's large cotton stocks and a lack of farmers' incentive to grow cotton, traders said.
"That's a far more serious problem than the weather," said a senior cotton trader.
China recently raised the state purchase price for standard ginned cotton to 700 yuan per 50 kg from 544 yuan in September 1995 to lure more farmers from higher-earning cash crops.
Another top government priority was dispersing growing commercial stocks, and lowering the domestic price of cotton would be the best way to do this, traders said.
Domestic Chinese cotton costs about 10 U.S. cents per lb more than the international market, which is currently quoted at about 84-86 U.S. cents per lb on a C&F China basis.
The government was in the process of discussing lowering the price of commercial stocks, but no decisions had been reached, one source said.
"Nobody is willing to buy new crop forward, because they don't know what is going to happen with China's commercial stockpile," the source said.
Industry sources agreed that China would probably have to make domestic cotton prices roughly the same as the international price to make it competitive.
Cotton mills in China frequently turn to cheaper, better quality imports, rather than dipping into domestic stocks.
"The pressure (to dissipate stocks) will mount as we get into September, when China's harvesting for the new crop comes on stream and warehousing space is needed for the new crop," a trader said.
But the cotton crop would definitely drop, they added, concurring with the official view.
China's official media have forecast China's cotton output for 1997 at 4.0 to 4.15 million tonnes, compared with 4.2 million tonnes last year.
